Sign uncertainty and de Branges spaces

Emanuel Carneiro , Tolibjon Ismoilov and Antonio Pedro Ramos Address: ICTP - The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics, Strada Costiera, 11, I - 34151, Trieste, Italy. Email address: carneiro@ictp.it Address: SISSA - Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati, Via Bonomea 265, 34136 Trieste, Italy Email address: tolibjon.ismoilov@sissa.it Email address: adeazeve@sissa.it
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We investigate here the sign uncertainty phenomenon for bandlimited functions, with a competing condition given by integration with respect to a general measure. Our main result provides a framework related to the theory of de Branges spaces of entire functions, that allows one to find the sharp constants and classify the extremizers in a broad range of situations. We discuss an application in number theory, in connection to bounds for zeros of LL-functions.

Key words and phrases: 
Sign uncertainty, bandlimited functions, de Branges spaces, reproducing kernel.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
46E22, 42A05, 42B35, 30H45, 33C10

1. Introduction

1.1. Background

The expression Fourier uncertainty is ubiquitous in the literature, generally embodying the paradigm that one cannot have an unrestricted control of a function and its Fourier transform simultaneously. Some uncertainty principles arise motivated by applications in analysis and related fields. A particularly relevant work for our purposes here is the one of Bourgain, Clozel and Kahane [3], in which they introduced the so-called sign Fourier uncertainty principle, and applied it in connection to the study of real zeros of zeta functions over number fields and bounds for the associated discriminants. In order to describe it, let us first recall the basic terminology.

Throughout this text, our normalization for the Fourier transform of a function F∈L1​(ℝd)F\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is F^(𝒚)=∫ℝde−2πi𝒙⋅𝒚F(𝒙)d𝒙\widehat{F}({\bm{y}})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-2\pi i{\bm{x}}\cdot{\bm{y}}}F({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}{\bm{x}}. We say that a function F:ℝd→ℝF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is eventually non-negative if F⁡(𝒙)≥0F({\bm{x}})\geq 0 for sufficiently large |𝒙||{\bm{x}}|. In this case, we define the radius of the last sign change of FF as

r⁡(F):=inf{r>0:F⁡(𝒙)≥0​for​|𝒙|≥r}.r(F):=\inf\{r>0\ :\ F({\bm{x}})\geq 0\ \,{\rm for}\ \,|{\bm{x}}|\geq r\}.

The sign Fourier uncertainty principle of [3] is the quest for the sharp constant

𝔸⁡(d):=inf0≠F∈𝒜⁡(d)r⁡(F)⋅r⁡(F^),\mathbb{A}(d):=\inf_{0\neq F\in\mathcal{A}(d)}\sqrt{r(F)\,\cdot\,r\big(\widehat{F}\,\big)}\,,

where the infimum is taken over the class 𝒜⁡(d)\mathcal{A}(d) of continuous and even functions F:ℝd→ℝF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} such that: (i) F,F^∈L1​(ℝd)F,\widehat{F}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}); (ii) F⁡(0)≤0F(0)\leq 0 and F^​(0)≤0\widehat{F}(0)\leq 0; (iii) FF and F^\widehat{F} are eventually non-negative. Note that the product r⁡(F)⋅r⁡(F^)r(F)\,\cdot\,r\big(\widehat{F}\,\big) is a natural quantity of interest since it is invariant under rescalings of the function FF. Bourgain, Clozel and Kahane [3] proved that

d2​π​e≤𝔸⁡(d)≤d+22​π\sqrt{\frac{d}{2\pi e}}\leq\mathbb{A}(d)\leq\sqrt{\frac{d+2}{2\pi}}

for any d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. In particular, 𝔸⁡(d)>0\mathbb{A}(d)>0, which is qualitatively the statement that, in this setup, the negative masses of FF and F^\widehat{F} cannot simultaneously concentrate near the origin. The only known sharp constant in this problem is due to Cohn and Gonçalves [11], who proved that 𝔸⁡(12)=2\mathbb{A}(12)=\sqrt{2}, using the machinery introduced by Viazovska [30] on Laplace transforms of modular forms. Extensions of this problem to a more abstract operator setting can be found in [15], and to a setup where the signs of FF and F^\widehat{F} resonate with a prescribed function in [10]. Other related works include [14] and [16].

1.2. A general problem for functions of exponential type

We aim to look at a related problem within the realm of sign uncertainty. In the previous setup, when restricted to the subclass of eventually non-negative bandlimited FF, with supp⁡(F^)⊂[−Δ,Δ]{\rm supp}(\widehat{F})\subset[-\Delta,\Delta] (for a Δ>0\Delta>0 prescribed), one could ask for the minimum value of r⁡(F)r(F) instead.

The Paley-Wiener theorem [29, Chapter III, Section 4] tells us that bandlimited functions are closely related to entire functions of exponential type in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}, and we can phrase our problem in this more general class. Vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} or ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d} are denoted here with bold font (e.g., 𝒙{\bm{x}}, 𝒚{\bm{y}}, 𝒛{\bm{z}}) and numbers in ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C} with regular font (e.g., x,y,zx,y,z). For 𝒛=(z1,z2,…,zd)∈ℂd{\bm{z}}=(z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{d})\in\mathbb{C}^{d} we let |⋅||\cdot| be the usual norm |𝒛|:=(|z1|2+…+|zd|2)1/2|{\bm{z}}|:=(|z_{1}|^{2}+\ldots+|z_{d}|^{2})^{1/2}, and define a second norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| by

∥𝒛∥:=sup{|∑n=1dzntn|;𝒕∈ℝdand|𝒕|≤1}.\|{\bm{z}}\|:=\sup\left\{\left|\sum_{n=1}^{d}z_{n}\,t_{n}\right|;\ {\bm{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\ {\rm and}\ |{\bm{t}}|\leq 1\right\}.

If F:ℂd→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} is an entire function of dd complex variables, which is not identically zero, we say that FF has exponential type if

τ⁡(F):=lim sup‖𝒛‖→∞‖𝒛‖−1​log⁡|F⁡(𝒛)|<∞.\tau(F):=\limsup_{\|{\bm{z}}\|\to\infty}\|{\bm{z}}\|^{-1}\,\log|F({\bm{z}})|<\infty.

In this case, the number τ⁡(F)\tau(F) is called the exponential type of FF. When d=1d=1 this is the classical definition of exponential type and, when d≥2d\geq 2, this definition is a particular case of a more general concept of exponential type with respect to a compact, convex and symmetric set K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (cf. [29, pp. 111-112]). In our case, this convex set KK is simply the unit Euclidean ball. With this definition, the Paley-Wiener theorem tells us that for F∈L2​(ℝd)F\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) the following are equivalent: (i) FF is equal a.e. to the restriction to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} of an entire function of exponential type at most δ\delta; and (ii) F^\widehat{F} is supported in the ball of radius δ/2​π\delta/2\pi centered at the origin.

Let μ\mu be a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure on ℝ\mathbb{R} and let μd\mu^{d} be its lift to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, namely the radial measure given in polar coordinates 𝒙=r​ω{\bm{x}}=r\omega by

(1.1) d​μd​(𝒙)=d​σd−1​(ω)​d​μ​(r),\displaystyle\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=\text{\rm d}\sigma_{d-1}(\omega)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(r)\,,

where r>0r>0, ω∈𝕊d−1\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, and σd−1\sigma_{d-1} is the standard surface measure on the unit sphere 𝕊d−1⊂ℝd\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (when d=1d=1, we simply have μ1=μ\mu^{1}=\mu). For instance, if d​μ​(x)=W⁡(x)​d​x\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=W(x)\,\text{\rm d}x, then d​μd​(𝒙)=|𝒙|1−d​W​(|𝒙|)​d​𝒙\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=|{\bm{x}}|^{1-d}\,W(|{\bm{x}}|)\,\text{\rm d}{\bm{x}}. We say that an entire function F:ℂd→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} is real entire when its restriction to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is real-valued. We consider here the following general problem.

Extremal Problem 1 (EP1): Given a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure μ\mu on ℝ\mathbb{R}, δ≥0\delta\geq 0 and d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, find11 1 Here the symbol F|ℝdF\arrowvert_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} denotes FF restricted to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

𝔼(μ;δ;d):=inf0≠F∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d)r(F|ℝd),\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;d):=\inf_{0\neq F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d)}r(F\arrowvert_{\mathbb{R}^{d}})\,,

where the infimum is taken over the class of functions

ℰ(μ;δ;d):={F:ℂd→ℂ​real entire of exponential type at most​δ;F∈L1​(ℝd,μd)and∫ℝdF⁡(𝒙)​d​μd​(𝒙)≤0;F|ℝdeventually non-negative.}.\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}F:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}\ \text{real entire of exponential type at most}\ \delta;\\ F\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mu^{d})\ \ {\rm and}\ \ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}F({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\leq 0;\\ F\arrowvert_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\ \text{eventually non-negative}.\end{array}\right\}.

With a slight abuse of notation, from now on we identify FF and F|ℝdF\arrowvert_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}, as it will be clear from the context when we are working on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Note the tension between the condition that FF is eventually non-negative on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} while ∫ℝdF⁡(𝒙)​d​μd​(𝒙)≤0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}F({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\leq 0. Note also the great generality allowed by the choice of the measure μ\mu. In fact, this problem came to our attention motivated by particular choices of measures μ\mu arising in applications in number theory; see §1.5.1 below. The condition of μ\mu being locally finite avoids the situation where all functions in the class ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d)\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d) need to vanish in a certain region. Note also that the class ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d)\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d) might be trivial (i.e., it only contains the identically zero function); this is the case, for instance, when d​μ​(x)=e|x|4​d​x\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=e^{|x|^{4}}\text{\rm d}x, by the classical Hardy’s uncertainty principle. Problems related to our (EP1), for bandlimited functions of a constant sign at infinity, have been considered in [17, 24, 25].

Our first result is that we can reduce matters to dimension d=1d=1.

Theorem 1 (Dimension shifts).

With the notation as above, we have

𝔼⁡(μ,δ,d)=𝔼⁡(μ,δ,1).\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;d)=\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;1).

The proof of Theorem 1 is carried out in Section 2 and relies on suitable radial symmetrization mechanisms. From now on, when working with d=1d=1, let us shorten the notation and simply write:

ℰ⁡(μ,δ):=ℰ⁡(μ,δ,1)and𝔼⁡(μ,δ):=𝔼⁡(μ,δ,1).\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta):=\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;1)\ \ \ {\rm and}\ \ \ \mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta):=\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;1).

1.3. Sign uncertainty and de Branges spaces

In some situations of interest, we connect the extremal problem (EP1) to the beautiful theory of de Branges spaces of entire functions [5]. Let us briefly review here some of the definitions from complex analysis in order to state our results; later in §3.1.1 we provide a more detailed discussion on de Branges spaces.

For an entire function F:ℂ→ℂF:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}, we define the entire function F∗:ℂ→ℂF^{*}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} by F∗​(z):=F⁡(z¯)¯F^{*}(z):=\overline{F(\overline{z})}. We denote by ℂ+={z∈ℂ;Im⁡(z)>0}\mathbb{C}^{+}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\ ;\ {\rm Im}(z)>0\} the open upper half-plane. A Hermite-Biehler function E:ℂ→ℂE:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} is an entire function that verifies the inequality

(1.2) |E∗​(z)|<|E⁡(z)||E^{*}(z)|<|E(z)|

for all z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}. We say that an analytic function F:ℂ+→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{+}\to\mathbb{C} has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+} if it can be written as the quotient of two functions that are analytic and bounded in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}. If F:ℂ+→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{+}\to\mathbb{C} has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}, from its Nevanlinna factorization [5, Theorems 9 and 10], one has

(1.3) v⁡(F):=lim supy→∞y−1​log⁡|F⁡(i​y)|<∞.v(F):=\limsup_{y\to\infty}\,y^{-1}\log|F(iy)|<\infty.

The number v⁡(F)v(F) is called the mean type of FF. If a Hermite-Biehler function EE has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}, then so does E∗E^{*}. In fact, if we write E=P/QE=P/Q with PP and QQ analytic and bounded in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}, we have E∗=((E∗/E)​P)/QE^{*}=((E^{*}/E)P)/Q and, by a result of Krein (Lemma 8 below), EE has exponential type and

τ⁡(E)=max⁡{v⁡(E),v⁡(E∗)}=v⁡(E),\tau(E)=\max\{v(E),v(E^{*})\}=v(E)\,,

where the last equality follows from (1.2) and (1.3).

Associated to a Hermite-Biehler function E:ℂ→ℂE:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}, one can consider the pair of real entire functions AA and BB such that E⁡(z)=A⁡(z)−i​B​(z)E(z)=A(z)-iB(z). These companion functions are given by

(1.4) A⁡(z):=12​(E⁡(z)+E∗​(z))andB⁡(z):=i2​(E⁡(z)−E∗​(z)),A(z):=\frac{1}{2}\big(E(z)+E^{*}(z)\big)\ \ \ {\rm and}\ \ \ B(z):=\frac{i}{2}\big(E(z)-E^{*}(z)\big)\,,

and note that they can only have real roots by (1.2).

We shall work here with a Hermite-Biehler function E:ℂ→ℂE:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} satisfying the following three conditions:

  • (C1)

    EE has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}.

  • (C2)

    The function z↦E⁡(i​z)z\mapsto E(iz) is real entire.

  • (C3)

    EE has no real zeros.

Note that (C2) is equivalent to the statement that AA is even and BB is odd, and (C3) is equivalent to that fact that AA and BB have no common zeros (in particular A⁡(0)≠0A(0)\neq 0). We consider measures μ\mu on ℝ\mathbb{R} that are related to the measure |E⁡(x)|−2​d​x|E(x)|^{-2}\text{\rm d}x in an integral sense given by the following condition:

  • (C4)

    For any real entire function F:ℂ→ℂF:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} of exponential type at most 2​τ​(E)2\tau(E), that is non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}, we have the identity

    (1.5) ∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x.

Of course, if

(1.6) d​μ​(x)=|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x\,,

condition (C4) is trivially verified. As we shall see, it is important for many applications to have the flexibility allowed by the integral condition (C4) rather than the pointwise condition (1.6).

The next result is the main result of this paper. We fully solve the extremal problem (EP1) in the following general situation.

Theorem 2 (Sharp constants).

Let E:ℂ→ℂE:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} be a Hermite-Biehler function verifying conditions (C1), (C2) and (C3) above. Let μ\mu be a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure on ℝ\mathbb{R} that verifies condition (C4). Let A:=12​(E+E∗)A:=\frac{1}{2}\big(E+E^{*}\big) and let ξ1\xi_{1} be the smallest positive real zero of AA. Then

𝔼⁡(μ, 2​τ​(E))=ξ1\mathbb{E}(\mu;\,2\tau(E))=\xi_{1}

and the unique extremizer (up to multiplication by a positive constant) is

(1.7) F⁡(z)=A​(z)2z2−ξ12.F(z)=\frac{A(z)^{2}}{z^{2}-\xi_{1}^{2}}.

Remarks: (i) In case AA does not have zeros, one may check that A⁡(z)=aA(z)=a and B⁡(z)=b​zB(z)=bz, and hence E⁡(z)=a−i​b​zE(z)=a-ibz, for certain a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} with a​b>0ab>0. In this case one can show that ℰ⁡(μ,0)={0}\mathcal{E}(\mu;0)=\{0\}.

(ii) From the proof of Theorem 1 we also get, for d>1d>1, that the unique extremizer (up to multiplication by a positive constant) of 𝔼⁡(μ,2​τ​(E),d)\mathbb{E}(\mu;2\tau(E);d), that is radial on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, is the lift of the function (1.7), as discussed in Section 2.

(iii) Note that the case of the Lebesgue measure and δ>0\delta>0 is a particular case of Theorem 2 for we can consider E(z)=e−iδz/2E(z)=e^{-i\delta z/2} to show that 𝔼⁡(d​x,δ)=π/δ\mathbb{E}(\text{\rm d}x;\delta)=\pi/\delta and the only extremizer (up to multiplication by a positive constant) is F⁡(z)=cos2⁡(δ​z/2)/(z2−(π/δ)2)F(z)=\cos^{2}(\delta z/2)/(z^{2}-(\pi/\delta)^{2}).

(iv) For a given measure μ\mu, there might be multiple Hermite-Biehler functions EE with the same exponential type that verify (C4); see the discussion in §5.1. The smallest positive zero of A:=12​(E+E∗)A:=\frac{1}{2}\big(E+E^{*}\big) is the same for all such EE.

We shall present two different proofs for Theorem 2 in Section 3. The first proof uses a basic polynomial lemma to reduce the search for extremizers to even functions with only one sign change in the positive axis, and in such a setup one can connect matters to a related extremal problem in de Branges spaces, concerning the multiplication by zz operator. The second proof makes use of certain quadrature formulas in this context of de Branges spaces.

1.4. A negative result

In §1.3 we have been interested in a broad situation where we can actually find the sharp version of the uncertainty principle in (EP1). In general, it is an interesting (and seemingly non-trivial) problem to find necessary and sufficient conditions on the measure μ\mu that would guarantee a qualitative sign uncertainty principle (i.e. the fact that 𝔼⁡(μ,δ)>0\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta)>0). Our next result shows that, if the measure μ\mu has a certain amount of mass around the origin and an exponential decay, the sign uncertainty does not hold.

Theorem 3.

Let μ\mu be a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure on ℝ\mathbb{R} such that:

  • (i)

    μ⁡([−r,r])>0\mu\big([-r,r]\big)>0 for each r>0r>0.

  • (ii)

    ∫ℝeε​|x|​d​μ​(x)<∞\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\varepsilon|x|}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)<\infty for some ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Then 𝔼⁡(μ,δ)=0\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta)=0 for any δ≥0\delta\geq 0.

In particular, if the measure μ\mu verifies (i) and has compact support, we fall under the hypotheses of Theorem 3. The conditions in Theorem 3 are sufficient but not necessary as the following example shows: if one considers μ⁡(x)=∑n∈ℤ𝜹⁡(x−n)\mu(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}{\bm{\delta}}(x-n), where 𝜹{\bm{\delta}} is the usual Dirac delta at the origin, the function F⁡(z)=sin2⁡(π​z)∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​π)F(z)=\sin^{2}(\pi z)\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\pi) and verifies r⁡(F)=0r(F)=0. If one prefers a function that is not identically zero μ\mu-a.e. one can consider instead F⁡(z)=(z2−ε2)​sin2⁡(π​z)/(π​z)2F(z)=(z^{2}-\varepsilon^{2})\sin^{2}(\pi z)/(\pi z)^{2} for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small.

1.5. Applications

We discuss here three applications of Theorem 2.

1.5.1. Bounds for low-lying zeros in families of LL-functions

The extremal problem (EP1) is related to the problem of bounding the height of the first zero in families of LL-functions. Let us very briefly discuss the setup for this problem; the reader can consult the references presented in this subsection for the technical details and a variety of examples.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a set of number theoretical objects (one can think of Dirichlet characters, for example) and assume that to each f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} one can associate an LL-function

L⁡(s,f)=∑n=1∞λf​(n)​n−s,L(s,f)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{f}(n)\,n^{-s}\,,

where the coefficients λf​(n)∈ℂ\lambda_{f}(n)\in\mathbb{C}. Assume that L⁡(s,f)L(s,f) admits an analytic continuation to an entire function. Let us denote the analytic conductor of L⁡(s,f)L(s,f) by cfc_{f} and write its non-trivial zeros as ρf=12+i​γf\rho_{f}=\frac{1}{2}+i\gamma_{f}. Assume also the validity of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for such LL-functions; i.e., that γf∈ℝ\gamma_{f}\in\mathbb{R}. The density conjecture of Katz and Sarnak [21, 22] asserts that for each natural family {L⁡(s,f),f∈ℱ}\{L(s,f),\ f\in\mathcal{F}\} of LL-functions there is an associated symmetry group G=G⁡(ℱCLOSEG=G(\mathcal{F}), where GG is either: unitary U{\rm U}, symplectic Sp{\rm Sp}, orthogonal O{\rm O}, even orthogonal SO⁡(even){\rm SO}(\rm{even}), or odd orthogonal SO⁡(odd){\rm SO}({\rm odd}). Here one wishes to consider averages over f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} ordered by the conductor. Following the notation of Iwaniec, Luo and Sarnak [20], let ℱ⁡(Q):={f∈ℱ:cf=Q}\mathcal{F}(Q):=\{f\in\mathcal{F}\,:\,c_{f}=Q\}22 2 One may also consider ℱ⁡(Q):={f∈ℱ:cf≤Q}\mathcal{F}(Q):=\{f\in\mathcal{F}\,:\,c_{f}\leq Q\} in some situations. and let |ℱ⁡(Q)||\mathcal{F}(Q)| denote its cardinality. If ϕ:ℝ→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is an even Schwartz function whose Fourier transform has compact support, Katz and Sarnak [21, 22] conjectured that

(1.8) limQ→∞1|ℱ⁡(Q)|​∑f∈ℱ⁡(Q)∑γfϕ⁡(γf​log⁡cf2​π)=∫ℝϕ⁡(x)​WG​(x)​d​x,\lim_{Q\to\infty}\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}(Q)|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}(Q)}\sum_{\gamma_{f}}\phi\!\left(\gamma_{f}\frac{\log c_{f}}{2\pi}\right)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(x)\,W_{G}(x)\,\text{\rm d}x,

where the sum over γf\gamma_{f} counts multiplicity, and WGW_{G} is a function (or density) depending on the symmetry group G⁡(ℱ)G(\mathcal{F}). This is the so-called 1-level density of the low-lying zeros of the family. For these five symmetry groups, Katz and Sarnak determined the density functions:

(1.9) WU​(x)=1;WSp​(x)=1−sin⁡2​π​x2​π​x;WO​(x)=1+12​𝜹​(x);WSO⁡(even)​(x)=1+sin⁡2​π​x2​π​x;WSO⁡(odd)​(x)=1−sin⁡2​π​x2​π​x+𝜹⁡(x).\begin{split}W_{\rm U}(x)&=1\ \ \ ;\ \ \ W_{\rm Sp}(x)=1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\ \ \ ;\ \ \ W_{\rm O}(x)=1+\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{\delta}(x)\,;\\ W_{{\rm SO}(\rm{even})}(x)&=1+\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\ \ \ ;\ \ \ W_{{\rm SO}({\rm odd})}(x)=1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}+\bm{\delta}(x).\end{split}

The simplest example would perhaps be when ℱ\mathcal{F} is the set of non-principal Dirichlet characters χ\chi (and here the analytic conductor of L⁡(s,χ)L(s,\chi) is just the modulus qq of χ\chi). In this case, Hughes and Rudnick [19] proved the validity of (1.8), with unitary symmetry G⁡(ℱ)=UG(\mathcal{F})={\rm U}, for even Schwartz functions ϕ:ℝ→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} with supp⁡(ϕ^)⊂[−2,2]{\rm supp}\big(\widehat{\phi}\,\big)\subset[-2,2]. There are several other results in the literature establishing the validity of (1.8) for different families of LL-functions and different sizes of the support of ϕ^\widehat{\phi}; see, for instance, [7, 12, 13, 19, 20, 27] and the references therein.

In this context, the analysis problem that arises is the following: assume the validity of (1.8) for even Schwartz functions ϕ:ℝ→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} with supp⁡(ϕ^)⊂[−Δ,Δ]{\rm supp}\big(\widehat{\phi}\,\big)\subset[-\Delta,\Delta], with Δ>0\Delta>0 fixed; what is the sharpest upper bound that one can get for the height of the first zero in the family as Q→∞Q\to\infty with this information? Under these assumptions, if ϕ\phi is such that ϕ⁡(x)≥0\phi(x)\geq 0 for |x|≥r|x|\geq r,  and ∫ℝϕ⁡(x)​WG​(x)​d​x<0\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(x)\,W_{G}(x)\,\text{\rm d}x<0, relation (1.8) plainly yields

lim supQ→∞minγff∈ℱ⁡(Q)⁡|γf​log⁡cf2​π|≤r.\limsup_{Q\to\infty}\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma_{f}\\ f\in\mathcal{F}(Q)\end{subarray}}\left|\frac{\gamma_{f}\,\log c_{f}}{2\pi}\right|\leq r.

Hence, one is led to the problem of finding the infimum over all such possible values of rr, which is exactly our extremal problem (EP1) in the case of the five measures μ\mu with densities given by (1.9)33 3 The fact that the functions are even and Schwartz, and that the integral is strictly less than 00, are harmless due to standard approximation arguments.. By the Paley-Wiener theorem one seeks here the constant 𝔼⁡(μ,2​π​Δ)\mathbb{E}(\mu;2\pi\Delta).

There are three previous works in the literature that address the problem of estimating the height of the first zero within this framework. The first one, by Hughes and Rudnick [19, Theorem 8.1], deals with the case of G⁡(ℱ)=UG(\mathcal{F})={\rm U}. The other two, by Bernard [2, Theorem 1 and Proposition 2] and by the first author with Chirre and Milinovich [7, Theorem 9], deal with the other measures. These papers have a common feature: they work under the additional assumption that ϕ\phi is of the form

(1.10) ϕ⁡(x)=(x2−r2)​ψ​(x)​ψ∗​(x),\phi(x)=(x^{2}-r^{2})\,\psi(x)\,\psi^{*}(x),

where ψ\psi is such that supp(ψ^)⊂[−Δ/2,Δ/2]{\rm supp}\big(\widehat{\psi}\,\big)\subset[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]. Within this more restrictive class, they arrive at the extremal solution. However, in principle, it is not obvious that one can restrict the search in the original problem to functions as in (1.10), which have only one sign change. The cases of these five measures with densities given by (1.9) fall under the general umbrella of our Theorem 2, and this provides a subtle, yet conceptually interesting, contribution to this framework, namely:

Corollary 4.

The additional assumption (1.10) brings no loss of generality in the search for 𝔼⁡(μ,2​π​Δ)\mathbb{E}(\mu;2\pi\Delta) in the cases of the measures μ\mu with densities given by (1.9).

Hence, the results obtained in [2, 7, 19] are in fact the extremal solutions in the larger class ℰ⁡(μ,2​π​Δ)\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\pi\Delta).

1.5.2. Power weights

An interesting situation in our framework is the following. Let ν>−1\nu>-1 and consider the locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure μν\mu_{\nu} on ℝ\mathbb{R} given by

(1.11) d​μν​(x)=|x|2​ν+1​d​x.\text{\rm d}\mu_{\nu}(x)=|x|^{2\nu+1}\text{\rm d}x.

Let JνJ_{\nu} be the classical Bessel function of the first kind. Then

(1.12) Aν​(z):=Γ⁡(ν+1)​(12​z)−ν​Jν​(z)=∑n=0∞(−1)n​(12​z)2​nn!​(ν+1)​(ν+2)​…​(ν+n)\displaystyle A_{\nu}(z):=\Gamma(\nu+1)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}z\right)^{-\nu}J_{\nu}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}z\big)^{2n}}{n!(\nu+1)(\nu+2)\ldots(\nu+n)}

defines an even entire function of exponential type 11. When ν=−1/2\nu=-1/2 (which is the case of the Lebesgue measure on ℝ\mathbb{R}) we simply have A−1/2(z)=coszA_{-1/2}(z)=\cos z. The following result comes as a corollary of our Theorem 2.

Corollary 5.

For ν>−1\nu>-1 let μv\mu_{v} be given by (1.11). Let 𝔧ν,1{\mathfrak{j}}_{\nu,1} be the first positive zero of the Bessel function JνJ_{\nu}. Then, for δ>0\delta>0,

𝔼⁡(μν,δ)=2​𝔧ν,1δ.\mathbb{E}(\mu_{\nu};\delta)=\frac{2\,{\mathfrak{j}}_{\nu,1}}{\delta}.

1.5.3. Measures asymptotically comparable to power weights

One may wonder how broad is the reach of Theorem 2. In fact, fairly general measures would fall under the scope of this theorem (and, in particular, the sign uncertainty principle holds), as our next result illustrates.

Corollary 6.

Let μ\mu be a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure on ℝ\mathbb{R}, given by

d​μ​(x)=W⁡(x)​d​x\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=W(x)\,\text{\rm d}x

on the set {x∈ℝ;|x|>R}\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,;\,|x|>R\} for some R>0R>0, where WW is a non-negative Borel measurable function. Assume further that

W⁡(x)≃|x|2​ν+1W(x)\simeq|x|^{2\nu+1}

on the set {x∈ℝ;|x|>R}\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,;\,|x|>R\}, for some ν>−1\nu>-1. Then, for any δ>0\delta>0, the problem of computing 𝔼⁡(μ,δ)\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta) falls under the framework of Theorem 2. In particular, 𝔼⁡(μ,δ)>0\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta)>0.

Remark: (i) Note that, in the setup of Corollary 6, for δ=0\delta=0 we have ℰ⁡(μ,0)={0}\mathcal{E}(\mu;0)=\{0\}.

2. Lifts and symmetrization: proof of Theorem 1

2.1. Preliminaries

The radial symmetry of the problem plays an important role in this argument, and we start by recalling two suitable constructions from the work of Holt and Vaaler [18, Section 6].

If G:ℂ→ℂG:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} is an even entire function with power series representation

G⁡(z)=∑k=0∞ck​z2​k,\displaystyle G(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}z^{2k}\,,

we define its lift to ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}, namely the function ℒd​(G):ℂd→ℂ{\mathcal{L}}_{d}(G):\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}, by

ℒd​(G)​(𝒛):=∑k=0∞ck​(z12+…+zd2)k.\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}_{d}(G)({{\bm{z}}}):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}(z_{1}^{2}+\ldots+z_{d}^{2})^{k}.

If d>1d>1 and F:ℂd→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} is an entire function, we define its radial symmetrization F~:ℂd→ℂ\widetilde{F}:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} by

F~​(𝒛):=∫S​O​(d)F⁡(R​𝒛)​d​η​(R),\widetilde{F}({\bm{z}}):=\int_{SO(d)}F(R{\bm{z}})\,\text{\rm d}\eta(R),

where S​O​(d)SO(d) denotes the compact topological group of real orthogonal d×dd\times d matrices with determinant 11, with associated Haar measure η\eta normalized so that η⁡(S​O​(d))=1\eta(SO(d))=1. If d=1d=1, we simply set F~​(z):=12​{F⁡(z)+F⁡(−z)}\widetilde{F}(z):=\tfrac{1}{2}\{F(z)+F(-z)\}.

The following result is a compilation of [18, Lemmas 18 and 19], and is concerned with the relation between these symmetrization mechanisms and the exponential type of the underlying functions.

Lemma 7.

The following propositions hold:

  • (i)

    Let G:ℂ→ℂG:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} be an even entire function. Then GG has exponential type if and only if ℒd​(G){\mathcal{L}}_{d}(G) has exponential type, and τ⁡(G)=τ⁡(ℒd​(G))\tau(G)=\tau({\mathcal{L}}_{d}(G)).

  • (ii)

    Let F:ℂd→ℂF:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} be an entire function. Then F~:ℂd→ℂ\widetilde{F}:\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} is an entire function with power series expansion of the form

    F~​(𝒛)=∑k=0∞ck​(z12+…+zd2)k.\widetilde{F}({{\bm{z}}})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}(z_{1}^{2}+\ldots+z_{d}^{2})^{k}.

    Moreover, if FF has exponential type then F~\widetilde{F} has exponential type and τ⁡(F~)≤τ⁡(F)\tau\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big)\leq\tau(F).

2.2. Proof of Theorem 1

Let F∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d)F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d). Then, from Lemma 7 (ii) we have that τ⁡(F~)≤τ⁡(F)≤δ\tau\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big)\leq\tau(F)\leq\delta. The fact that FF is real entire, not identically zero and eventually non-negative implies that F~\widetilde{F} is also real entire, not identically zero and eventually non-negative, and we plainly have r⁡(F~)≤r⁡(F)r\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big)\leq r(F). Using Fubini’s theorem and the fact that μd\mu^{d} is rotationally invariant, we have

(2.1) ∫ℝd|F~​(𝒙)|​d​μd​(𝒙)≤∫ℝd∫S​O​(d)|F⁡(R​𝒙)|​d​η​(R)​d​μd​(𝒙)=∫S​O​(d)∫ℝd|F⁡(R​𝒙)|​d​μd​(𝒙)​d​η​(R)=∫S​O​(d)∫ℝd|F⁡(𝒙)|​d​μd​(𝒙)​d​η​(R)=∫ℝd|F⁡(𝒙)|​d​μd​(𝒙).\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big|\widetilde{F}({\bm{x}})\big|\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})&\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{SO(d)}|F(R{\bm{x}})|\,\text{\rm d}\eta(R)\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\\ &=\int_{SO(d)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|F(R{\bm{x}})|\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\eta(R)\\ &=\int_{SO(d)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|F({\bm{x}})|\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\eta(R)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|F({\bm{x}})|\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}}).\end{split}

Hence F~∈L1​(ℝd,μd)\widetilde{F}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mu^{d}). An identical computation to (2.1), without the absolute values, yields

∫ℝdF~​(𝒙)​d​μd​(𝒙)=∫ℝd∫S​O​(d)F⁡(R​𝒙)​d​η​(R)​d​μd​(𝒙)=∫ℝdF⁡(𝒙)​d​μd​(𝒙)≤0.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\widetilde{F}({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{SO(d)}F(R{\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\eta(R)\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}F({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})\leq 0.

We then conclude that F~∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d)\widetilde{F}\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d) (in sum, we can restrict ourselves to real entire functions that are radial on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} without loss of generality).

Using Lemma 7 we see that F~=ℒd​(G)\widetilde{F}={\mathcal{L}}_{d}(G) for a certain G:ℂ→ℂG:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} real entire, even, eventually non-negative, and with τ⁡(G)=τ⁡(F~)≤δ\tau(G)=\tau\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big)\leq\delta. Moreover, from (1.1) we have

(2.2) ∫ℝd|F~​(𝒙)|​d​μd​(𝒙)=∫0∞∫𝕊d−1|G⁡(r)|​d​σd−1​(ω)​d​μ​(r)=ωd−12​∫ℝ|G⁡(x)|​d​μ​(x),\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\big|\widetilde{F}({\bm{x}})\big|\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{{\mathbb{S}}^{d-1}}|G(r)|\,\text{\rm d}\sigma_{d-1}(\omega)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(r)=\frac{\omega_{d-1}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|G(x)|\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\,,

where ωd−1\omega_{d-1} is the surface area of 𝕊d−1{\mathbb{S}}^{d-1}, and hence G∈L1​(ℝ,μ)G\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu). Similarly,

(2.3) 0≥∫ℝdF~​(𝒙)​d​μd​(𝒙)=∫0∞∫𝕊d−1G⁡(r)​d​σd−1​(ω)​d​μ​(r)=ωd−12​∫ℝG⁡(x)​d​μ​(x),\displaystyle 0\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\widetilde{F}({\bm{x}})\,\text{\rm d}\mu^{d}({\bm{x}})=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{{\mathbb{S}}^{d-1}}G(r)\,\text{\rm d}\sigma_{d-1}(\omega)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(r)=\frac{\omega_{d-1}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\,,

and we conclude that G∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,1)G\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;1). Since r⁡(G)=r⁡(F~)r(G)=r\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big) we arrive at the inequality

(2.4) 𝔼⁡(μ,δ,1)≤𝔼⁡(μ,δ,d).\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;1)\leq\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;d).

Conversely, starting now with H∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,1)H\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;1), since the measure μ\mu is even, we can replace it by H~​(z):=12​{H⁡(z)+H⁡(−z)}\widetilde{H}(z):=\tfrac{1}{2}\{H(z)+H(-z)\} that verifies r⁡(H~)≤r⁡(H)r\big(\widetilde{H}\,\big)\leq r(H). We then consider the lift ℒd​(H~){\mathcal{L}}_{d}\big(\widetilde{H}\big), and note that Lemma 7 and computations as in (2.2) and (2.3) show that ℒd​(H~)∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ,d){\mathcal{L}}_{d}\big(\widetilde{H}\big)\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta;d). Since r⁡(H~)=r⁡(ℒd​(H~))r\big(\widetilde{H}\big)=r\big({\mathcal{L}}_{d}\big(\widetilde{H}\big)\big), we arrive at the inequality

(2.5) 𝔼⁡(μ,δ,d)≤𝔼⁡(μ,δ,1).\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;d)\leq\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta;1).

The result now follows from (2.4) and (2.5).

3. De Branges spaces and the proof of Theorem 2

3.1. Preliminaries

We start by reviewing some of the basic elements from the theory of de Branges spaces, and collecting a few lemmas from the literature that will be important for our purposes.

3.1.1. De Branges spaces

We provide a brief overview, building up on the material introduced in §1.3. For a detailed exposition we refer the reader to [5, Chapters I and II].

Given a Hermite-Biehler function E:ℂ→ℂE:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}, the de Branges space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) associated to EE is the space of entire functions F:ℂ→ℂF:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} such that

(3.1) ‖F‖ℋ⁡(E)2:=∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x<∞,\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x<\infty\,,

and such that F/EF/E and F∗/EF^{*}/E have bounded type and non-positive mean type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}. This is a Hilbert space with inner product given by

⟨F,G⟩ℋ⁡(E):=∫ℝF⁡(x)​G⁡(x)¯​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x.\langle F,G\rangle_{\mathcal{H}(E)}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\overline{G(x)}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x.

In fact, this is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. That is, for each w∈ℂw\in\mathbb{C} the evaluation functional F↦F⁡(w)F\mapsto F(w) is bounded on ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) or, equivalently, by the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a function K⁡(w,⋅)∈ℋ⁡(E)K(w,\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}(E) such that

F⁡(w)=⟨F,K⁡(w,⋅)⟩ℋ⁡(E)F(w)=\langle F,K(w,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}(E)}

for all F∈ℋ⁡(E)F\in\mathcal{H}(E). Writing E⁡(z)=A⁡(z)−i​B​(z)E(z)=A(z)-iB(z) with AA and BB real entire as in (1.4), the reproducing kernel K⁡(w,⋅)K(w,\cdot), is given by (see [5, Theorem 19])

(3.2) K⁡(w,z)=B⁡(z)​A​(w¯)−A⁡(z)​B​(w¯)π⁡(z−w¯),K(w,z)=\frac{B(z)A(\overline{w})-A(z)B(\overline{w})}{\pi(z-\overline{w})}\,,

and, when z=w¯z=\overline{w},

K⁡(z¯,z)=B′​(z)​A​(z)−A′​(z)​B​(z)π.K(\overline{z},z)=\frac{B^{\prime}(z)A(z)-A^{\prime}(z)B(z)}{\pi}.

We shall only be interested in the situation where K⁡(w,w)=‖K⁡(w,⋅)‖ℋ⁡(E)2>0K(w,w)=\|K(w,\cdot)\|^{2}_{\mathcal{H}(E)}>0 for all w∈ℂw\in\mathbb{C}, which is equivalent (see [18, Lemma 11]) to the statement that EE has no real zeros. A phase function φ:ℝ→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} associated with EE is a continuous function such that E⁡(x)​ei​φ​(x)E(x)e^{i\varphi(x)} is real for all values of xx. In this case,

φ′​(x)=π​K​(x,x)|E⁡(x)|2>0.\varphi^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\pi\,K(x,x)}{|E(x)|^{2}}>0.

If α\alpha is a given real number, the solutions of φ⁡(ξ)≡α⁡(mod​π)\varphi(\xi)\equiv\,\alpha\,{\rm(mod\ }\pi{\rm)} correspond to the zeros (which must be real and simple) of the real entire function

(3.3) Tα​(z):=ei​α​E​(z)−e−i​α​E∗​(z)2​i.\displaystyle T_{\alpha}(z):=\frac{e^{i\alpha}E(z)-e^{-i\alpha}E^{*}(z)}{2i}.

Note that the zeros of any two TαT_{\alpha} and TβT_{\beta} interlace. With this notation, observe that T0=−BT_{0}=-B and Tπ/2=AT_{\pi/2}=A. Observe also that there is at most one real number α\alpha modulo π\pi such that Tα∈ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{H}(E) (otherwise we would have E∈ℋ⁡(E)E\in\mathcal{H}(E), which would contradict (3.1)). One of the cornerstones of the theory is the following orthogonality result [5, Theorem 22]: the set of functions Γα:={K⁡(ξ,⋅);Tα​(ξ)=0}\Gamma_{\alpha}:=\{K(\xi,\cdot)\ ;T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0\} is always an orthogonal set in ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E); if Tα∉ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\notin\mathcal{H}(E), the set Γα\Gamma_{\alpha} is an orthogonal basis of ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) and, if Tα∈ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{H}(E), the only elements of ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) that are orthogonal to Γα\Gamma_{\alpha} are the constant multiples of TαT_{\alpha}. In particular, if Tα∉ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\notin\mathcal{H}(E), for every F∈ℋ⁡(E)F\in\mathcal{H}(E) we have

(3.4) F⁡(z)=∑Tα​(ξ)=0F⁡(ξ)K⁡(ξ,ξ)​K​(ξ,z)and‖F‖ℋ⁡(E)2=∑Tα​(ξ)=0|F⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ).F(z)=\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{F(\xi)}{K(\xi,\xi)}\,K(\xi,z)\ \ \ {\rm and}\ \ \ \|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}=\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{\big|F(\xi)\big|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}.

3.1.2. Krein’s memoir

We recall a result of M. G. Krein [23] that allows us to relate the condition of bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+} to the condition of exponential type in ℂ\mathbb{C}. Recall that log+|x|:=max⁡{0,log⁡|x|}\log^{+}|x|:=\max\{0,\log|x|\}.

Lemma 8 (Krein).

Let F:ℂ→ℂF:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} be an entire function. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    FF and F∗F^{*} have bounded type in the open upper half-plane ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}.

  2. (ii)

    FF has exponential type and

    ∫ℝlog+⁡|F⁡(x)|1+x2​d​x<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\log^{+}|F(x)|}{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}x<\infty.

If either and therefore both of these conditions hold then τ⁡(F)=max⁡{v⁡(F),v⁡(F∗)}\tau(F)=\max\{v(F),v(F^{*})\}.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote the set of entire functions FF which satisfy one and therefore both of the conditions (i) or (ii) in Lemma 8. The next result can be proved using Lemma 8 and is contained in [18, Lemma 12]. It allows us to easily characterize the de Branges space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) when EE has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}.

Lemma 9.

Let EE be a Hermite-Biehler function of bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}, and FF be an entire function. Then EE belongs to ℬ\mathcal{B} and the following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    F∈ℋ⁡(E)F\in\mathcal{H}(E).

  • (ii)

    F∈ℬF\in\mathcal{B}, max⁡{v⁡(F),v⁡(F∗)}≤v⁡(E)\max\{v(F),v(F^{*})\}\leq v(E) and (3.1) holds.

  • (ii)

    FF has exponential type, τ⁡(F)≤τ⁡(E)\tau(F)\leq\tau(E) and (3.1) holds.

Moreover, if ξ\xi is real and 0<K⁡(ξ,ξ)0<K(\xi,\xi), the entire function K⁡(ξ,⋅)∈ℋ⁡(E)K(\xi,\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}(E) verifies τ⁡(K⁡(ξ,⋅))=τ⁡(E)\tau(K(\xi,\cdot))=\tau(E).

Our final preliminary lemma in this subsection is [9, Lemma 14], a factorization result for real entire functions of exponential type that are non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. This is an important tool to connect the L1L^{1} and the L2L^{2} theories in our context.

Lemma 10.

Let EE be a Hermite-Biehler function of bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+} with exponential type τ⁡(E)\tau(E). Let F:ℂ→ℂF:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} be a real entire function of exponential type at most 2​τ​(E)2\tau(E) that satisfies

F⁡(x)≥0\displaystyle F(x)\geq 0

for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and

∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x<∞.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x<\infty.

Then there exists U∈ℋ⁡(E)U\in\mathcal{H}(E) such that

F⁡(z)=U⁡(z)​U∗​(z)\displaystyle F(z)=U(z)\,U^{*}(z)

for all z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}.

3.1.3. Polynomial reductions

We consider in this subsection a basic auxiliary result that allows us to reduce the search for extremizers in our extremal problem (EP1) to functions that have only one sign change. The next proposition is related to [28, Problem 45, Part VI] and we provide here a short proof for the reader’s convenience.

Proposition 11.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 be an integer and let 0<t1<t2<…<tn0<t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{n} be distinct positive real numbers. If PP is the monic polynomial defined by

P⁡(x)=∏k=1n(x2−tk2),P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x^{2}-t_{k}^{2}),

then, for any positive number r>tnr>t_{n}, there exist even polynomials QQ and RR, both non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}, satisfying the following properties:

  • (i)

    P⁡(x)=(x2−r2)​Q​(x)+R⁡(x)P(x)=(x^{2}-r^{2})Q(x)+R(x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}.

  • (ii)

    deg⁡(Q)={2​n−2, if ​n​ is odd;2​n−4, if ​n​ is even;{\rm deg}(Q)=\begin{cases}2n-2,&\textit{ if }n\textit{ is odd;}\\ 2n-4,&\textit{ if }n\textit{ is even;}\end{cases} and deg⁡(R)={2​n−2, if ​n​ is odd;2​n, if ​n​ is even.{\rm deg}(R)=\begin{cases}2n-2,&\textit{ if }n\textit{ is odd;}\\ 2n,&\textit{ if }n\textit{ is even.}\end{cases}

Proof.

We prove this by induction on nn. At each step we show how to construct the polynomials Q=QnQ=Q_{n} and R=RnR=R_{n} (it should be clear to the reader that these polynomials depend not only on nn but on t1,t2,…,tnt_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n} and rr as well). If n=1n=1 and 0<t1<r0<t_{1}<r, note that

P⁡(x)=x2−t12=(x2−r2)⋅1+(r2−t12).P(x)=x^{2}-t_{1}^{2}=(x^{2}-r^{2})\cdot 1+(r^{2}-t_{1}^{2}).

In this case we can take Q1​(x):=1Q_{1}(x):=1 and R1​(x):=r2−t12R_{1}(x):=r^{2}-t_{1}^{2}, which are polynomials of degree 0.

Now let n=2n=2 and 0<t1<t2<r0<t_{1}<t_{2}<r. Since P⁡(x)=(x2−t12)​(x2−t22)P(x)=(x^{2}-t_{1}^{2})(x^{2}-t_{2}^{2}), we can apply the previous case to each of the factors as follows

P⁡(x)=((x2−r2)​Q1​(x)+R1​(x))​((x2−r2)⋅1+(r2−t22))=(x2−r2)​{R1​(x)+(r2−t22)​Q1​(x)}+{(x2−r2)2​Q1​(x)+(r2−t22)​R1​(x)}.\begin{split}P(x)&=\big((x^{2}-r^{2})\,Q_{1}(x)+R_{1}(x)\big)\left((x^{2}-r^{2})\cdot 1+(r^{2}-t_{2}^{2})\right)\\ &=(x^{2}-r^{2})\left\{R_{1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{2}^{2})\,Q_{1}(x)\right\}+\left\{(x^{2}-r^{2})^{2}\,Q_{1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{2}^{2})\,R_{1}(x)\right\}.\\ \end{split}

In this case we can take Q2​(x):=R1​(x)+(r2−t22)​Q1​(x)Q_{2}(x):=R_{1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{2}^{2})\,Q_{1}(x) and R2​(x):=(x2−r2)2​Q1​(x)+(r2−t22)​R1​(x)R_{2}(x):=(x^{2}-r^{2})^{2}\,Q_{1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{2}^{2})\,R_{1}(x). Note that since deg⁡(Q1)=deg⁡(R1)=0{\rm deg}(Q_{1})={\rm deg}(R_{1})=0 we have deg⁡(Q2)=0{\rm deg}(Q_{2})=0 and deg⁡(R2)=4{\rm deg}(R_{2})=4.

Assume that the assertion holds for all n≤N−1n\leq N-1, for some integer N≥3N\geq 3. Consider the case n=Nn=N, with 0<t1<t2<…<tN−1<tN<r0<t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{N-1}<t_{N}<r and write

(3.5) P⁡(x)=(x2−tN2)​∏k=1N−1(x2−tk2).P(x)=(x^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(x^{2}-t_{k}^{2}).

By the induction hypothesis, there exist even polynomials QN−1​(x)Q_{N-1}(x) and RN−1​(x)R_{N-1}(x), both non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}, such that

(3.6) ∏k=1N−1(x2−tk2)=(x2−r2)​QN−1​(x)+RN−1​(x).\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(x^{2}-t_{k}^{2})=(x^{2}-r^{2})\,Q_{N-1}(x)+R_{N-1}(x).

On the other hand, the factor (x2−tN2)(x^{2}-t_{N}^{2}) falls into the scope of the case n=1n=1; i.e.,

(3.7) x2−tN2=(x2−r2)⋅1+(r2−tN2).x^{2}-t_{N}^{2}=(x^{2}-r^{2})\cdot 1+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2}).

Combining (3.5), (3.6) and (3.7) we get

P⁡(x)\displaystyle P(x) =((x2−r2)​QN−1​(x)+RN−1​(x))​((x2−r2)⋅1+(r2−tN2))\displaystyle=\big((x^{2}-r^{2})\,Q_{N-1}(x)+R_{N-1}(x)\big)\,\big((x^{2}-r^{2})\cdot 1+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\big)
=(x2−r2)​{RN−1​(x)+(r2−tN2)​QN−1​(x)}+{(x2−r2)2​QN−1​(x)+(r2−tN2)​RN−1​(x)}\displaystyle=(x^{2}-r^{2})\left\{R_{N-1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\,Q_{N-1}(x)\right\}+\left\{(x^{2}-r^{2})^{2}\,Q_{N-1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\,R_{N-1}(x)\right\}
=(x2−r2)​QN​(x)+RN​(x),\displaystyle=(x^{2}-r^{2})\,Q_{N}(x)+R_{N}(x),

where QN​(x):=RN−1​(x)+(r2−tN2)​QN−1​(x)Q_{N}(x):=R_{N-1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\,Q_{N-1}(x) and RN​(x):=(x2−r2)2​QN−1​(x)+(r2−tN2)​RN−1​(x)R_{N}(x):=(x^{2}-r^{2})^{2}\,Q_{N-1}(x)+(r^{2}-t_{N}^{2})\,R_{N-1}(x). Note that QNQ_{N} and RNR_{N} are both even and non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Also, by the induction hypothesis,

deg⁡(QN)=max⁡{deg⁡(QN−1),deg⁡(RN−1)}=deg⁡(RN−1)={2​N−4, if ​N​ is even;2​N−2, if ​N​ is odd;{\rm deg}(Q_{N})=\max\big\{{\rm deg}(Q_{N-1}),{\rm deg}(R_{N-1})\big\}={\rm deg}(R_{N-1})=\begin{cases}2N-4,&\textnormal{ if }N\textnormal{ is even;}\\ 2N-2,&\textnormal{ if }N\textnormal{ is odd;}\end{cases}

and

deg⁡(RN)=max⁡{4+deg⁡(QN−1),deg⁡(RN−1)}=4+deg⁡(QN−1)={2​N, if ​N​ is even;2​N−2, if ​N​ is odd.{\rm deg}(R_{N})=\max\big\{4+{\rm deg}(Q_{N-1}),{\rm deg}(R_{N-1})\big\}=4+{\rm deg}(Q_{N-1})=\begin{cases}2N,&\textnormal{ if }N\textnormal{ is even;}\\ 2N-2,&\textnormal{ if }N\textnormal{ is odd.}\end{cases}

This concludes the proof. ∎

With the aid of Proposition 11 we establish the following reduction in the search for extremizers in problem (EP1).

Proposition 12.

Let F∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ)F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta) be an even function and set r:=r⁡(F)r:=r(F). Then there exists G∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ)G\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta) of the form G⁡(z)=(z2−r2)​H​(z)G(z)=(z^{2}-r^{2})H(z), where HH is an even and real entire function of exponential type at most δ\delta that is non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. In particular, note that r⁡(G)=r⁡(F)r(G)=r(F).

Proof.

Since FF is even and belongs to ℰ⁡(μ,δ)\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta), it has only finitely many sign changes on the positive axis. If it has only one sign change, we are done. If not, we label these as 0<t1<t2<…<tn<r0<t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots<t_{n}<r and write

(3.8) F⁡(x)=(∏k=1n(x2−tk2))​(x2−r2)​F1​(x),F(x)=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x^{2}-t_{k}^{2})\right)(x^{2}-r^{2})\,F_{1}(x)\,,

where F1F_{1} is an even and real entire function of exponential type at most δ\delta that is non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. We apply Proposition 11 to the product from k=1k=1 to nn in (3.8) and observe that

(3.9) F⁡(x)=((x2−r2)​Q​(x)+R⁡(x))​(x2−r2)​F1​(x)=(x2−r2)2​Q​(x)​F1​(x)+(x2−r2)​R​(x)​F1​(x)≥(x2−r2)​R​(x)​F1​(x)\displaystyle\begin{split}F(x)&=\Big((x^{2}-r^{2})Q(x)+R(x)\Big)(x^{2}-r^{2})\,F_{1}(x)\\ &=(x^{2}-r^{2})^{2}\,Q(x)F_{1}(x)+(x^{2}-r^{2})R(x)F_{1}(x)\\ &\geq(x^{2}-r^{2})R(x)F_{1}(x)\end{split}

for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Let G⁡(z):=(z2−r2)​R​(z)​F1​(z)G(z):=(z^{2}-r^{2})R(z)F_{1}(z). By Proposition 11 we have deg⁡(R)≤2​n{\rm deg}(R)\leq 2n and hence

(3.10) |R⁡(x)|≲|∏k=1n(x2−tk2)||R(x)|\lesssim\left|\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x^{2}-t_{k}^{2})\right|

for |x||x| large. Since F∈L1​(ℝ,μ)F\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu), from (3.10) and the fact that μ\mu is locally finite we conclude that G∈L1​(ℝ,μ)G\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu). Moreover, from (3.9) we plainly have

0≥∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)≥∫ℝG⁡(x)​d​μ​(x).0\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x).

Hence, G∈ℰ⁡(μ,δ)G\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta), as desired. ∎

3.2. Proof of Theorem 2

We are now in position to present our first proof of Theorem 2. Assume now that we are considering a measure μ\mu and a Hermite-Biehler function EE that verify the conditions (C1), (C2), (C3) and (C4).

3.2.1. Reduction to an L2L^{2}-extremal problem

As already observed in the proof of Theorem 1, if we start with F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)), we can consider F~​(z):=12​{F⁡(z)+F⁡(−z)}\widetilde{F}(z):=\tfrac{1}{2}\{F(z)+F(-z)\} that verifies F~∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))\widetilde{F}\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) (since μ\mu is even) and r⁡(F~)≤r⁡(F)r\big(\widetilde{F}\,\big)\leq r(F). Hence, for the purposes of finding the sharp constant, we can restrict our search to even functions. We have seen in Proposition 12 that we can further restrict our search to functions G∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))G\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) of the form G⁡(z)=(z2−r2)​H​(z)G(z)=(z^{2}-r^{2})H(z), with HH even, real entire of exponential type at most 2​τ​(E)2\tau(E), and non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Since x2​H​(x)∈L1​(ℝ,μ)x^{2}H(x)\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu) (recall that μ\mu is locally finite), condition (C4) yields

(3.11) 0≥∫ℝG⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=(∫ℝx2​H​(x)​d​μ​(x))−r2​(∫ℝH⁡(x)​d​μ​(x))=(∫ℝx2​H​(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)−r2​(∫ℝH⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)=∫ℝG⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}0\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)&=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2}H(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)-r^{2}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}H(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)\\ &=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2}H(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x\right)-r^{2}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}H(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x\right)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x.\end{split}

Since H∈L1​(ℝ,|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)H\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x) (from condition (C4)), we may use Lemma 10 to decompose H=U​U∗H=UU^{*}, with U∈ℋ⁡(E)U\in\mathcal{H}(E). Hence, as in (3.11), the fact that 0≥∫ℝG⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)0\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x) is equivalent to the fact that

r2≥∫ℝx2​|U⁡(x)|2​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x∫ℝ|U⁡(x)|2​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x=‖z​U‖ℋ⁡(E)2‖U‖ℋ⁡(E)2.r^{2}\geq\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2}\,|U(x)|^{2}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x}{\int_{\mathbb{R}}|U(x)|^{2}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x}=\frac{\|z\,U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}}{\|U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}}.

As our task is to minimize rr, we have reduced our extremal problem (EP1) to the following extremal problem related to multiplication by zz in a general de Branges space.

Extremal Problem 2 (EP2): Let EE be a Hermite-Biehler function. Find

𝕄z​(E):=inf0≠U∈ℋ⁡(E)‖z​U‖ℋ⁡(E)‖U‖ℋ⁡(E).\mathbb{M}_{z}(E):=\inf_{0\neq U\in\mathcal{H}(E)}\frac{\|z\,U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}}{\|U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}}.

It turns out that this problem has recently been addressed in the work of the first author with Chirre and Milinovich [7, Theorem 14], for EE verifying conditions (C2) and (C3) (note that condition (C1) was already used above when we invoked Lemma 10). We discuss its solution in the next subsection.

3.2.2. Solution of the extremal problem (EP2)

We recall here the result in [7, Theorem 14] and briefly reproduce its proof for the reader’s convenience. An extension of this result, computing the analogous infimum related to multiplication by zkz^{k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, was obtained in [8].

Proposition 13 (cf. [7]).

Let EE be a Hermite-Biehler function verifying conditions (C2) and (C3). Let A:=12​(E+E∗)A:=\frac{1}{2}\big(E+E^{*}\big) and let ξ1\xi_{1} be the smallest positive real zero of AA. Then

𝕄z​(E)=ξ1.\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)=\xi_{1}.

The unique extremizer (up multiplication by a non-zero complex constant) is

(3.12) U⁡(z)=A⁡(z)z2−ξ12.U(z)=\frac{A(z)}{z^{2}-\xi_{1}^{2}}.

Remark: If AA has no zeros then, from the discussion in §3.1.1, the space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) has dimension at most 11 and there are no functions U∈ℋ⁡(E)U\in\mathcal{H}(E) such that z​U∈ℋ⁡(E)zU\in\mathcal{H}(E).

Proof.

Let 𝒳⁡(E):={U∈ℋ⁡(E):z​U∈ℋ⁡(E)}\mathcal{X}(E):=\{U\in\mathcal{H}(E)\,:\,zU\in\mathcal{H}(E)\}, and recall that B=i2​(E−E∗)B=\frac{i}{2}\big(E-E^{*}\big). The proof considers two cases: when A∉ℋ⁡(E)A\notin\mathcal{H}(E) (a typical situation), and when A∈ℋ⁡(E)A\in\mathcal{H}(E) (an exceptional situation).

We first consider the case A∉ℋ⁡(E)A\notin\mathcal{H}(E). In this case, if 0≠U∈𝒳⁡(E)0\neq U\in\mathcal{X}(E), from (3.4) we have

(3.13) ‖U‖ℋ⁡(E)2=∑A⁡(ξ)=0|U⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)≤1ξ12​∑A⁡(ξ)=0|ξ|2​|U⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)=1ξ12​‖z​U‖ℋ⁡(E)2.\displaystyle\|U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}=\sum_{A(\xi)=0}\frac{\big|U(\xi)\big|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}\leq\frac{1}{\xi_{1}^{2}}\sum_{A(\xi)=0}\frac{|\xi|^{2}\,\big|U(\xi)\big|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}=\frac{1}{\xi_{1}^{2}}\,\|zU\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}.

This shows that 𝕄z​(E)≥ξ1\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)\geq\xi_{1}. In order to have equality in (3.13) one must have U⁡(ξ)=0U(\xi)=0 for each zero ξ\xi of AA with ξ≠±ξ1\xi\neq\pm\xi_{1}. By the interpolation formula in (3.4) (recall that K⁡(ξ1,ξ1)=K⁡(−ξ1,−ξ1)K(\xi_{1},\xi_{1})=K(-\xi_{1},-\xi_{1}) in our setup) we get

(3.14) U⁡(z)\displaystyle U(z) =1K⁡(ξ1,ξ1)​(U⁡(ξ1)​K​(ξ1,z)+U⁡(−ξ1)​K​(−ξ1,z)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K(\xi_{1},\xi_{1})}\big(U(\xi_{1})\,K(\xi_{1},z)+U(-\xi_{1})\,K(-\xi_{1},z)\big).

From (3.14) and (3.2) one can write

(3.15) z​U​(z)=A⁡(z)​B​(ξ1)π​K​(ξ1,ξ1)​(U⁡(−ξ1)−U⁡(ξ1))+ξ1​U​(ξ1)K⁡(ξ1,ξ1)​K​(ξ1,z)+(−ξ1)​U​(−ξ1)K⁡(ξ1,ξ1)​K​(−ξ1,z).zU(z)=\frac{A(z)B(\xi_{1})}{\pi K(\xi_{1},\xi_{1})}\big(U(-\xi_{1})-U(\xi_{1})\big)+\frac{\xi_{1}\,U(\xi_{1})}{K(\xi_{1},\xi_{1})}K(\xi_{1},z)+\frac{(-\xi_{1})\,U(-\xi_{1})}{K(\xi_{1},\xi_{1})}K(-\xi_{1},z).

From (3.15), one now observes that z​U∈ℋ⁡(E)zU\in\mathcal{H}(E) if and only if U⁡(ξ1)=U⁡(−ξ1)U(\xi_{1})=U(-\xi_{1}). This leads to the conclusion that 𝕄z​(E)=ξ1\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)=\xi_{1}, with extremizers as in (3.12).

We now consider the exceptional case A∈ℋ⁡(E)A\in\mathcal{H}(E). By [5, Theorem 29] a function G∈ℋ⁡(E)G\in\mathcal{H}(E) is orthogonal to the subspace 𝒳⁡(E)\mathcal{X}(E) if and only if it is of the form G⁡(z)=α​A​(z)+β​B​(z)G(z)=\alpha A(z)+\beta B(z) for constants α,β∈ℂ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C}. If there is such a function GG with β≠0\beta\neq 0, then B∈ℋ⁡(E)B\in\mathcal{H}(E), and hence E∈ℋ⁡(E)E\in\mathcal{H}(E), contradicting (3.1). Therefore 𝒳​(E)⟂=span⁡{A}\mathcal{X}(E)^{\perp}={\rm span}\{A\}. Recalling the discussion at the end of §3.1.1, that Tπ/2=AT_{\pi/2}=A and Γπ/2∪{A}\Gamma_{\pi/2}\cup\{A\} is an orthogonal basis of ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E), if 0≠U∈𝒳⁡(E)0\neq U\in\mathcal{X}(E) we have

(3.16) ‖U‖ℋ⁡(E)2=∑A⁡(ξ)=0|U⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)≤1ξ12​∑A⁡(ξ)=0|ξ|2​|U⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)≤1ξ12​‖z​U‖ℋ⁡(E)2,\displaystyle\|U\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}=\sum_{A(\xi)=0}\frac{\big|U(\xi)\big|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}\leq\frac{1}{\xi_{1}^{2}}\sum_{A(\xi)=0}\frac{|\xi|^{2}\,\big|U(\xi)\big|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}\leq\frac{1}{\xi_{1}^{2}}\,\|zU\|_{\mathcal{H}(E)}^{2}\,,

which shows that 𝕄z​(E)≥ξ1\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)\geq\xi_{1}. Equality in (3.16) occurs if and only if U⁡(ξ)=0U(\xi)=0 for each zero ξ\xi of AA with ξ≠±ξ1\xi\neq\pm\xi_{1}, and z​U⟂AzU\perp A. As we are assuming that U∈𝒳⁡(E)U\in\mathcal{X}(E), we have that U⟂AU\perp A, which implies that UU has a representation as in (3.14). From (3.15) one sees that z​U⟂AzU\perp A if and only if U⁡(ξ1)=U⁡(−ξ1)U(\xi_{1})=U(-\xi_{1}), which leads us to the conclusion that 𝕄z​(E)=ξ1\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)=\xi_{1}, with extremizers as in (3.12). ∎

In light of the discussion in §3.2.1 and Proposition 13, we arrive at the conclusion that

𝔼⁡(μ, 2​τ​(E))=𝕄z​(E)=ξ1,\mathbb{E}(\mu;\,2\tau(E))=\mathbb{M}_{z}(E)=\xi_{1},

as desired.

3.2.3. Classification of the extremizers

The discussion in §3.2.1 and §3.2.2 also leads us to the following conclusion: if G∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))G\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) is an even extremizer that has only one sign change on the positive real axis at ξ1\xi_{1}, then GG must be of the form (1.7).

Observe that any even function F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) verifies

(3.17) ∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x.

This follows from condition (C4), by writing FF as a difference of two functions that are non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R} and belong to L1​(ℝ,μ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu) (looking at the factorization (3.8), this plainly follows by writing an even polynomial as a difference of two polynomials that are non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}). Now assume that F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) is an even extremizer that has more than one sign change on the positive real axis (i.e. n≥1n\geq 1 in the factorization (3.8)). One then notices that the inequality F⁡(x)≥G⁡(x)F(x)\geq G(x) in (3.9) is strict for a.e. x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. In light of (3.17), we are led to the fact that

(3.18) 0≥∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x>∫ℝG⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x=∫ℝG⁡(x)​d​μ​(x).\displaystyle 0\geq\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x>\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x=\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x).

Finally, we need to show that all extremizers must be even. If F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) is a generic extremizer, we have seen that F~​(z):=12​{F⁡(z)+F⁡(−z)}\widetilde{F}(z):=\tfrac{1}{2}\{F(z)+F(-z)\} is an even extremizer, and hence given by (1.7). So, we want to show that if

3.3. Alternative proof of Theorem 2

This second proof makes use of certain quadrature formulas in our context of de Branges spaces. It is slightly more direct than our first proof (although we are going to invoke some elements from the proof of Proposition 13). On the other hand, the polynomial reduction used in the first proof has the advantage that it can also be used for general measures μ\mu. Here we again consider a measure μ\mu and a Hermite-Biehler function EE that verify the conditions (C1), (C2), (C3) and (C4). We also assume that AA has at least one zero.

3.3.1. Quadrature formulas

First observe that there exists a real entire function MM of exponential type at most 2​τ​(E)2\tau(E) that is strictly positive on ℝ\mathbb{R} and verifies M∈L1​(ℝ,|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)M\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},|E(x)|^{-2}\text{\rm d}x) (which, by (C4), is equivalent to M∈L1​(ℝ,μ)M\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu)). Take, for instance,

M⁡(z)=K​(ξ1,z)2+K​(0,z)2=B​(ξ1)2​A​(z)2π2​(z−ξ1)2+A​(0)2​B​(z)2π2​z2.M(z)=K(\xi_{1},z)^{2}+K(0,z)^{2}=\frac{B(\xi_{1})^{2}A(z)^{2}}{\pi^{2}(z-\xi_{1})^{2}}+\frac{A(0)^{2}B(z)^{2}}{\pi^{2}z^{2}}.

Now, for each F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)), there is a positive constant c=cFc=c_{F} such that F+c​MF+cM is non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Then F+c​M∈L1​(ℝ,μ)F+cM\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu) and, by (C4), F+c​M∈L1​(ℝ,|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)F+cM\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},|E(x)|^{-2}\text{\rm d}x). In particular, F∈L1​(ℝ,|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x)F\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},|E(x)|^{-2}\text{\rm d}x). Using (C4) again, we have

(3.22) ∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=∫ℝ(F⁡(x)+c​M​(x))​d​μ​(x)−∫ℝc​M​(x)​d​μ​(x)=∫ℝ(F⁡(x)+c​M​(x))​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x−∫ℝc​M​(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x=∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(F(x)+cM(x)\big)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)-\int_{\mathbb{R}}cM(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(F(x)+cM(x)\big)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x-\int_{\mathbb{R}}cM(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x.\end{split}

Using Lemma 10, we can write F+c​M=U​U∗F+cM=UU^{*} and c​M=V​V∗cM=VV^{*} with U,V∈ℋ⁡(E)U,V\in\mathcal{H}(E), thus arriving at the representation

(3.23) F=U​U∗−V​V∗.\displaystyle F=UU^{*}-VV^{*}.

For α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, let TαT_{\alpha} be as in (3.3). If Tα∉ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\notin\mathcal{H}(E), from (3.23) and (3.4) we get

(3.24) ∫ℝF⁡(x)​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x=∫ℝ|U⁡(x)|2​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x−∫ℝ|V⁡(x)|2​|E⁡(x)|−2​d​x=∑Tα​(ξ)=0|U⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)−∑Tα​(ξ)=0|V⁡(ξ)|2K⁡(ξ,ξ)=∑Tα​(ξ)=0F⁡(ξ)K⁡(ξ,ξ).\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|U(x)|^{2}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x-\int_{\mathbb{R}}|V(x)|^{2}\,|E(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x\\ &=\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{|U(\xi)|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}-\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{|V(\xi)|^{2}}{K(\xi,\xi)}\\ &=\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{F(\xi)}{K(\xi,\xi)}.\end{split}

Hence, from (3.22) and (3.24), we arrive at the quadrature formula

(3.25) ∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=∑Tα​(ξ)=0F⁡(ξ)K⁡(ξ,ξ).\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=\sum_{T_{\alpha}(\xi)=0}\frac{F(\xi)}{K(\xi,\xi)}.

3.3.2. Finding the sharp constant

Assume that there exists F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) such that r⁡(F)<ξ1r(F)<\xi_{1}. Then there is an interval (a,b)⊂(r⁡(F),ξ1)(a,b)\subset(r(F),\xi_{1}) in which FF is strictly positive. As discussed in §3.1.1, choose α\alpha such that Tα∉ℋ⁡(E)T_{\alpha}\notin\mathcal{H}(E) and TαT_{\alpha} has a zero ζ∈(a,b)\zeta\in(a,b). Note that such a TαT_{\alpha} will have no other zero in the interval (−ξ1,ξ1)(-\xi_{1},\xi_{1}) by the interlacing property of the zeros. This plainly contradicts (3.25), since the left-hand side is non-positive by hypothesis, while the right-hand side is strictly positive. Hence, 𝔼⁡(μ, 2​τ​(E))≥ξ1\mathbb{E}(\mu;\,2\tau(E))\geq\xi_{1}.

In order to see that the function FF given by (1.7) verifies ∫ℝF⁡(x)​d​μ​(x)=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=0, we can argue as in the proof of Proposition 13. In the generic case when A=Tπ/2∉ℋ⁡(E)A=T_{\pi/2}\notin\mathcal{H}(E) we can, alternatively, use (3.25) directly. This shows that 𝔼⁡(μ, 2​τ​(E))=ξ1\mathbb{E}(\mu;\,2\tau(E))=\xi_{1}.

3.3.3. Classification of the extremizers

Let F∈ℰ⁡(μ,2​τ​(E))F\in\mathcal{E}(\mu;2\tau(E)) be an extremizer for our problem. Arguing as in §3.3.2, we conclude that FF cannot take strictly positive values in the interval (−ξ1,ξ1)(-\xi_{1},\xi_{1}). In particular, since FF is continuous, we must have F⁡(±ξ1)=0F(\pm\xi_{1})=0. This means that FF can be factored as F⁡(z)=(z2−ξ12)​H​(z)F(z)=(z^{2}-\xi_{1}^{2})H(z), with HH real entire, of exponential type at most 2​τ​(E)2\tau(E), and non-negative on ℝ\mathbb{R}. From condition (C4), we may use Lemma 10 to decompose H=U​U∗H=UU^{*}, with U∈ℋ⁡(E)U\in\mathcal{H}(E). Then, arguing as in the proof of Proposition 13 we arrive at the conclusion that FF must be given by (1.7).

4. Absence of sign uncertainty: proof of Theorem 3

4.1. Density of polynomials

We start with the following auxiliary result.

Lemma 14.

Let μ\mu be a locally finite, even and non-negative Borel measure on ℝ\mathbb{R} such that

(4.1) ∫ℝeε​|x|​d​μ​(x)<∞\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\varepsilon|x|}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)<\infty

for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then the space of polynomials is dense in L2​(ℝ,(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))L^{2}\big(\mathbb{R},(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\big).

Proof.

Let f∈L2​(ℝ,(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))f\in L^{2}\big(\mathbb{R},(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\big) be such that

(4.2) ∫ℝf⁡(x)​xk​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)\,x^{k}(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=0

for each k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\ldots. From (4.1) and an application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we have

∫ℝ|f⁡(x)​(1+x2)|​d​μ​(x)≤(∫ℝ(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))12​(∫ℝ|f⁡(x)|2​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))12<∞.\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|f(x)(1+x^{2})|\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\leq\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|f(x)|^{2}(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}<\infty.\end{split}

Hence f⁡(x)​(1+x2)∈L1​(ℝ,μ)f(x)(1+x^{2})\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mu). For ε>0\varepsilon>0 as in (4.1), let Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon} be the region in the complex plane given by Ωε:={z∈ℂ:|Im⁡(z)|<ε8​π}\Omega_{\varepsilon}:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|{\rm Im}(z)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{8\pi}\right\}, and define

F⁡(z):=∫ℝe−2​π​i​z​x​f​(x)​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x),forz∈Ωε.F(z):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-2\pi izx}f(x)(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x),\quad{\rm for}\ \ z\in\Omega_{\varepsilon}.

Note that for each z∈Ωεz\in\Omega_{\varepsilon} we have

(4.3) |F⁡(z)|≤∫ℝ|e−2​π​i​z​x||f⁡(x)|(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)≤∫ℝeε4​|x|​|f⁡(x)|​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)≲∫ℝeε2​|x|​|f⁡(x)|​1+x2​d​μ​(x)≤(∫ℝeε​|x|​d​μ​(x))12​(∫ℝ|f⁡(x)|2​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))12<∞.\begin{split}|F(z)|&\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left\lvert e^{-2\pi izx}\right\rvert|f(x)|\,(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\lvert x\rvert}|f(x)|\,(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\\ &\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\lvert x\rvert}|f(x)|\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\\ &\leq\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\varepsilon\lvert x\rvert}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|f(x)|^{2}(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}<\infty.\end{split}

Hence, FF defines an analytic function in Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon} by Morera’s theorem.

Using (4.3) (for the absolute convergence), Fubini’s theorem, and (4.2), we have, for each z∈Ωεz\in\Omega_{\varepsilon} with |z|<ε8​π|z|<\frac{\varepsilon}{8\pi},

F⁡(z)=∫ℝ(∑k=0∞(−2​π​i​z​x)kk!)​f​(x)​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)=∑k=0∞(−2​π​i​z)kk!​∫ℝf⁡(x)​xk​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)=0.\displaystyle F(z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-2\pi izx)^{k}}{k!}\right)f(x)(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-2\pi iz)^{k}}{k!}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)\,x^{k}(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)=0.

Since FF is analytic on Ωε\Omega_{\varepsilon}, we conclude that F=0F=0 in this region. Since FF is the Fourier transform of the finite Borel measure f⁡(x)​(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)f(x)(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x), we conclude that this measure must be identically zero. This in turn implies that f=0f=0 in L2​(ℝ,(1+x2)​d​μ​(x))L^{2}\big(\mathbb{R},(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\big), as desired. ∎

4.2. Proof of Theorem 3

Let μ1\mu_{1} be the measure given by d​μ1​(x)=(1+x2)​d​μ​(x)\text{\rm d}\mu_{1}(x)=(1+x^{2})\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x). Fix 0<r<20<r<2 and let η=η⁡(r)>0\eta=\eta(r)>0 to be chosen later. Using Lemma 14, let PP be a polynomial such that

(4.4) ‖P−𝟏[−r,r]‖L2​(ℝ,μ1)≤η.\displaystyle\big\|P-{\bf 1}_{[-r,r]}\big\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\,\mu_{1})}\leq\eta.

Note that

(4.5) ∫ℝ(x2−r2)​|P⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x)≤∫[−r,r]c(x2+1)|P(x)|2dμ(x)+∫−r/2r/2(x2−r2)|P(x)|2dμ(x)≤∥P−𝟏[−r,r]∥2L2​(ℝ,μ1)+((r2)2−r2)∫−r/2r/2|P(x)|2dμ(x)≤η2−(3​r24)12∫−r/2r/2(1+x2)|P(x)|2dμ(x).\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(x^{2}-r^{2})\,|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)&\leq\int_{[-r,r]^{c}}(x^{2}+1)\,|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)+\int_{-r/2}^{r/2}(x^{2}-r^{2})\,|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\\ &\leq\big\|P-{\bf 1}_{[-r,r]}\big\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\,\mu_{1})}+\left(\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{2}-r^{2}\right)\int_{-r/2}^{r/2}|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\\ &\leq\eta^{2}-\left(\frac{3r^{2}}{4}\right)\,\frac{1}{2}\int_{-r/2}^{r/2}(1+x^{2})|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x).\end{split}

From the triangle inequality and (4.4) we get

|‖P‖L2​([−r2,r2],μ1)−‖𝟏‖L2​([−r2,r2],μ1)|≤‖P−𝟏‖L2​([−r2,r2],μ1)≤‖P−𝟏[−r,r]‖L2​(ℝ,μ1)≤η,\displaystyle\big|\|P\|_{L^{2}([-\frac{r}{2},\frac{r}{2}],\,\mu_{1})}-\|{\bf 1}\|_{L^{2}([-\frac{r}{2},\frac{r}{2}],\,\mu_{1})}\big|\leq\|P-{\bf 1}\|_{L^{2}([-\frac{r}{2},\frac{r}{2}],\,\mu_{1})}\leq\big\|P-{\bf 1}_{[-r,r]}\big\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\,\mu_{1})}\leq\eta,

and hence

(4.6) ‖P‖L2​([−r2,r2],μ1)≥‖𝟏‖L2​([−r2,r2],μ1)−η=μ1​([−r2,r2])−η.\displaystyle\|P\|_{L^{2}([-\frac{r}{2},\frac{r}{2}],\,\mu_{1})}\geq\|{\bf 1}\|_{L^{2}([-\frac{r}{2},\frac{r}{2}],\,\mu_{1})}-\eta=\sqrt{\mu_{1}\big([-\tfrac{r}{2},\tfrac{r}{2}]\big)}-\eta.

From (4.5) and (4.6) we obtain

(4.7) ∫ℝ(x2−r2)​|P⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x)≤η2−3​r28​(μ1​([−r2,r2])−η)2.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}(x^{2}-r^{2})\,|P(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\leq\eta^{2}-\frac{3r^{2}}{8}\left(\sqrt{\mu_{1}\big([-\tfrac{r}{2},\tfrac{r}{2}]\big)}-\eta\right)^{2}.

Then the function F⁡(z)=(z2−r2)​P​(z)​P∗​(z)F(z)=(z^{2}-r^{2})P(z)P^{*}(z) belongs to the class ℰ⁡(μ,δ)\mathcal{E}(\mu;\delta) and r⁡(F)=rr(F)=r. Since rr was arbitrary, we conclude that 𝔼⁡(μ,δ)=0\mathbb{E}(\mu;\delta)=0.

5. Applications

5.1. Preliminaries

The following alternative characterization of de Branges spaces is given by [5, Theorem 23].

Lemma 15 (cf. [5]).

Let HH be a Hilbert space of entire functions that contains a non-zero element and verifies the following hypotheses:

  1. (i)

    If F∈HF\in H and has a non-real zero ww, the function z↦F⁡(z)​(z−w¯)/(z−w)z\mapsto F(z)(z-\overline{w})/(z-w) also belongs to HH and has the same norm of FF.

  2. (ii)

    For every non-real number ww, the linear functional defined on HH by F↦F⁡(w)F\mapsto F(w) is continuous.

  3. (iii)

    If F∈HF\in H, the function F∗F^{*} also belongs to HH and has the same norm of FF.

Then HH is equal isometrically to some de Branges space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E).

We have seen in §3.1.1 how to construct the KK from EE. An observation that is important for applications is the fact that we can revert this process and construct EE from KK (not necessarily in a unique way). This works as follows: if KK is the reproducing kernel of a Hilbert space HH verifying the conditions of Lemma 15, define the function

(5.1) L⁡(w,z):=2​π​i​(w¯−z)​K​(w,z),L(w,z):=2\pi i(\overline{w}-z)K(w,z)\,,

and the entire function

(5.2) E⁡(z):=L⁡(i,z)L​(i,i)12.E(z):=\frac{L(i,z)}{L(i,i)^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

One can show that EE is a Hermite-Biehler function such that

L⁡(w,z)=E⁡(z)​E∗​(w¯)−E∗​(z)​E​(w¯),L(w,z)=E(z)E^{*}(\overline{w})-E^{*}(z)E(\overline{w})\,,

and that HH is equal isometrically to the de Branges space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E). See [6, Appendix A] for details.

5.2. Proof of Corollary 4

For Δ>0\Delta>0 and WW one of the density functions given by (1.9), one can consider the Hilbert space HH of entire functions FF of exponential type at most Δ\Delta such that

‖F‖H:=(∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​W​(x)​d​x)1/2<∞.\displaystyle\|F\|_{H}:=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,W(x)\,\text{\rm d}x\right)^{1/2}<\infty.

The usual Paley-Wiener space P​W​(Δ)PW(\Delta) is the (reproducing kernel) Hilbert space of entire functions FF of exponential type at most Δ\Delta such that

‖F‖P​W​(Δ):=‖F‖L2​(ℝ)=(∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​d​x)1/2<∞.\displaystyle\|F\|_{PW(\Delta)}:=\|F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x\right)^{1/2}<\infty.

One sees that HH and P​W​(Δ)PW(\Delta) are equal as sets (since the density function WW is asymptotically 11). Moreover, due to classical uncertainty principles for the Fourier transform, one can show that

‖F‖H≃‖F‖L2​(ℝ).\|F\|_{H}\simeq\|F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}.

See [7, Section 3] for details. We then conclude that HH is also a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and fits into the hypotheses of Lemma 15.

It is shown in [7, §4.1] that the reproducing kernel KK of HH verifies the following properties, for all w,z∈ℂw,z\in\mathbb{C}: (i) K⁡(w,w)>0K(w,w)>0;   (ii) K⁡(−w,−z)=K⁡(w,z)K(-w,-z)=K(w,z);   (iii) K⁡(z,w)=K⁡(w,z)¯K(z,w)=\overline{K(w,z)};   (iv) K⁡(w¯,z¯)¯=K⁡(w,z)\overline{K(\overline{w},\overline{z})}=K(w,z). It then follows that EE defined by (5.1) - (5.2) verifies conditions (C2) and (C3) (if E⁡(w)=0E(w)=0 for w∈ℝw\in\mathbb{R}, one would have K⁡(w,w)=0K(w,w)=0). Since K⁡(i,z)K(i,z) has exponential type, so does EE. Also, since K⁡(i,z)K(i,z) belongs to L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), we may use Jensen’s inequality to obtain

(5.3) 1π​∫ℝlog+⁡|E⁡(x)|1+x2​d​x≤12​π​∫ℝlog⁡(1+|E⁡(x)|)21+x2​d​x≤12​log⁡(1+1π​∫ℝ|E⁡(x)|21+x2​d​x)<∞.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\log^{+}|E(x)|}{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}x\leq\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\log\big(1+|E(x)|\big)^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}x\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{|E(x)|^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}x\right)<\infty.

Hence, EE verifies the conditions of Lemma 8, which implies it has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+} (condition (C1)). From Lemma 9 we have τ⁡(E)=τ⁡(K⁡(0,⋅))\tau(E)=\tau(K(0,\cdot)), which is at most Δ\Delta. In fact, we must have τ⁡(E)=Δ\tau(E)=\Delta, since by Lemma 9 the space H=ℋ⁡(E)H=\mathcal{H}(E) admits only functions FF with τ⁡(F)≤τ⁡(E)\tau(F)\leq\tau(E), and we know from the start that there exist functions in P​W​(Δ)PW(\Delta) with exponential type equal to Δ\Delta. Finally, condition (C4) follows from the classical Krein’s factorization in P​W​(Δ)PW(\Delta) or Lemma 10, depending if we start with the left-hand side or the right-hand side of (1.5) being finite, and the fact that HH is isometric to ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E).

The conclusion is that this situation falls in the framework of Theorem 2, as claimed.

5.3. Proof of Corollary 5

Let ν>−1\nu>-1. A de Branges space ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) is said to be homogeneous of order ν\nu if, for all 0<a<10<a<1 and all f∈ℋ⁡(E)f\in\mathcal{H}(E), the function z↦aν+1​f​(a​z)z\mapsto a^{\nu+1}f(az) belongs to ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E) and has the same norm as ff. Such spaces were characterized by L. de Branges in [4] (see also [5, Section 50]).

Let AνA_{\nu} be the even real entire function defined in (1.12). We consider an odd real entire function BνB_{\nu} given by

Bν​(z)=Γ⁡(ν+1)​(12​z)−ν​Jν+1​(z)=∑n=0∞(−1)n​(12​z)2​n+1n!​(ν+1)​(ν+2)​…​(ν+n+1).\displaystyle B_{\nu}(z)=\Gamma(\nu+1)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}z\right)^{-\nu}J_{\nu+1}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}z\big)^{2n+1}}{n!(\nu+1)(\nu+2)\ldots(\nu+n+1)}.

Then the function

Eν​(z):=Aν​(z)−i​Bν​(z)E_{\nu}(z):=A_{\nu}(z)-iB_{\nu}(z)

turns out to be a Hermite-Biehler function of bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}, with no real zeros, and ℋ⁡(Eν)\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) is homogeneous of order ν\nu. Moreover we have τ⁡(Aν)=τ⁡(Bν)=τ⁡(Eν)=1\tau(A_{\nu})=\tau(B_{\nu})=\tau(E_{\nu})=1. Note also that Aν,Bν∉ℋ⁡(Eν)A_{\nu},B_{\nu}\notin\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) (for this one can look at the behaviour of the Bessel function JνJ_{\nu} at infinity). We refer the reader to [5, Section 50], [18, Section 5] or [9, Sections 3 and 4] for details. Some properties of the spaces ℋ⁡(Eν)\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) that are relevant for our purposes are collected in the next lemma, which is contained in [18, Eqs. (5.1), (5.2) and Lemma 16].

Lemma 16.

Let ν>−1\nu>-1. The following properties hold:

  1. (i)

    There exist positive constants aν,bνa_{\nu},b_{\nu} such that

    aν​|x|2​ν+1≤|Eν​(x)|−2≤bν​|x|2​ν+1\displaystyle a_{\nu}|x|^{2\nu+1}\leq|E_{\nu}(x)|^{-2}\leq b_{\nu}|x|^{2\nu+1}

    for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} with |x|≥1|x|\geq 1.

  2. (ii)

    For F∈ℋ⁡(Eν)F\in\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) we have the identity

    ∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|Eν​(x)|−2​d​x=cν​∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x,\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|E_{\nu}(x)|^{-2}\,\text{\rm d}x=c_{\nu}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\,,

    with cν=π​ 2−2​ν−1​Γ​(ν+1)−2c_{\nu}=\pi\,2^{-2\nu-1}\,\Gamma(\nu+1)^{-2}.

  3. (iii)

    An entire function FF belongs to ℋ⁡(Eν)\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) if and only if FF has exponential type at most 11 and

    ∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x<\infty.

This leads us to the conclusion that EνE_{\nu} verifies conditions (C1), (C2), (C3) and, with the aid of Lemma 16 and Lemma 10, one also verifies (C4). We then fall in the framework of Theorem 2, and the corollary follows (note that one can go from exponential type 11 to an arbitrary exponential type δ>0\delta>0 with a dilation argument).

5.4. Proof of Corollary 6

We proceed with the proof for δ=1\delta=1. For a generic exponential type δ>0\delta>0, one simply needs to consider the function z↦Eν​(δ​z)z\mapsto E_{\nu}(\delta z) in the proof below.

Let HH be the space of entire functions FF of exponential type at most 11 such that

‖F‖H:=(∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x))1/2<∞.\displaystyle\|F\|_{H}:=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\right)^{1/2}<\infty.

From Lemma 16 and the hypotheses of Corollary 6, one sees that HH and ℋ⁡(Eν)\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) are equal as sets. The next piece of information required for this proof is the following result.

Proposition 17.

Under the hypotheses of Corollary 6 we have

(5.4) ‖F‖H≃‖F‖ℋ⁡(Eν).\displaystyle\|F\|_{H}\simeq\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}.
Proof.

Let Kν​(w,z)K_{\nu}(w,z) be the reproducing kernel of the space ℋ⁡(Eν)\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}). If F∈H=ℋ⁡(Eν)F\in H=\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) one has the following pointwise bound, as a consequence of the reproducing kernel property and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

(5.5) |F(x)|2=|⟨F,Kν(x,⋅))⟩ℋ⁡(Eν)|2≤∥F∥ℋ⁡(Eν)2∥Kν(x,⋅)∥ℋ⁡(Eν)2=∥F∥ℋ⁡(Eν)2Kν(x,x).\displaystyle|F(x)|^{2}=\big|\langle F,K_{\nu}(x,\cdot))\rangle_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}\big|^{2}\leq\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}\,\big\|K_{\nu}(x,\cdot)\big\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}=\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}\,K_{\nu}(x,x).

Then, from (5.5), the hypotheses of Corollary 6, and Lemma 16,

∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x)\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x) =∫|x|≤R|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x)+∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{|x|\leq R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)+\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)
≲‖F‖ℋ⁡(Eν)2​∫|x|≤RKν​(x,x)​d​μ​(x)+∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x\displaystyle\lesssim\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}\int_{|x|\leq R}K_{\nu}(x,x)\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)+\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x
≲‖F‖ℋ⁡(Eν)2.\displaystyle\lesssim\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}.

This accounts for one of the inequalities needed to prove (5.4).

For the other inequality we argue as follows. If ν≥−1/2\nu\geq-1/2, we have that F∈H=ℋ⁡(Eν)F\in H=\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) implies F∈L2​(ℝ)F\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) and, from the Paley-Wiener theorem, supp⁡(F^)⊂[−12​π,12​π]{{\rm supp}}(\widehat{F})\subset[-\tfrac{1}{2\pi},\tfrac{1}{2\pi}]. Then, from the classical Amrein-Berthier-Nazarov uncertainty principle for the Fourier transform [1, 26] (see, alternatively, [8, Lemma 9]),

(5.6) ∫|x|≤R|F⁡(x)|2​d​x≲∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​d​x.\displaystyle\int_{|x|\leq R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x\lesssim\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x.

From (5.6) we get

∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x ≤R2​ν+1​∫|x|≤R|F⁡(x)|2​d​x+∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x\displaystyle\leq R^{2\nu+1}\int_{|x|\leq R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x+\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x
≲R2​ν+1​∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​d​x+∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x\displaystyle\lesssim R^{2\nu+1}\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x+\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x
≲∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x
≲∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x),\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x),

which is the desired inequality due to Lemma 16 (ii).

Now we consider the case −1<ν<−1/2-1<\nu<-1/2. For 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, using (5.5) we get

(5.7) ∫|x|<ε|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≤‖F‖ℋ⁡(Eν)2​∫|x|<εKν​(x,x)​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≤(max|x|≤1⁡Kν​(x,x)​∫|x|<ε|x|2​ν+1​d​x)​‖F‖ℋ⁡(Eν)2.\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{|x|<\varepsilon}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x&\leq\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}\int_{|x|<\varepsilon}K_{\nu}(x,x)\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\\ &\leq\left(\max_{|x|\leq 1}K_{\nu}(x,x)\int_{|x|<\varepsilon}|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\right)\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})}^{2}.\end{split}

Hence, from Lemma 16 (ii) and (5.7), we can choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, independently of FF, such that

(5.8) ∫|x|<ε|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≤∫|x|≥ε|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{|x|<\varepsilon}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\leq\int_{|x|\geq\varepsilon}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x.\end{split}

Now consider the entire function EαE_{\alpha}, with α=−ν−1\alpha=-\nu-1, that has exponential type at most 11. Note from Lemma 16 (i) that

|Eα​(x)|2≃|x|2​ν+1\displaystyle|E_{\alpha}(x)|^{2}\simeq|x|^{2\nu+1}

for |x|≥ε|x|\geq\varepsilon (we extended the range from |x|≥1|x|\geq 1 to |x|≥ε|x|\geq\varepsilon simply by noting that EαE_{\alpha} has no real zeros). We then note that F∈H=ℋ⁡(Eν)F\in H=\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) implies that F​Eα∈L2​(ℝ)F\,E_{\alpha}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) and has exponential type at most 22. An application of the Amrein-Berthier-Nazarov uncertainty principle [1, 26] yields

(5.9) ∫ε≤|x|≤R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≲∫ε≤|x|≤R|F⁡(x)​Eα​(x)|2​d​x≲∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)​Eα​(x)|2​d​x≲∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x.\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\varepsilon\leq|x|\leq R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x&\lesssim\int_{\varepsilon\leq|x|\leq R}|F(x)E_{\alpha}(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x\\ &\lesssim\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)E_{\alpha}(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}x\lesssim\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x.\end{split}

Then, (5.8) and (5.9) plainly lead to

∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≲∫|x|>R|F⁡(x)|2​|x|2​ν+1​d​x≲∫ℝ|F⁡(x)|2​d​μ​(x),\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\lesssim\int_{|x|>R}|F(x)|^{2}\,|x|^{2\nu+1}\,\text{\rm d}x\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x)|^{2}\,\text{\rm d}\mu(x)\,,

as desired. This concludes the proof. ∎

From Proposition 17 we conclude that HH is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and the conditions to invoke Lemma 15 are in place. Letting KK be the reproducing kernel of the Hilbert space HH, one can show (as done in [7, §4.1]), since the measure μ\mu is even, that KK verifies the following properties, for all w,z∈ℂw,z\in\mathbb{C}: (i) K⁡(w,w)>0K(w,w)>0;   (ii) K⁡(−w,−z)=K⁡(w,z)K(-w,-z)=K(w,z);   (iii) K⁡(z,w)=K⁡(w,z)¯K(z,w)=\overline{K(w,z)};   (iv) K⁡(w¯,z¯)¯=K⁡(w,z)\overline{K(\overline{w},\overline{z})}=K(w,z). From this it follows that EE defined by (5.1) - (5.2) verifies conditions (C2) and (C3). Since log+⁡|a​b|≤log+⁡|a|+log+⁡|b|\log^{+}|ab|\leq\log^{+}|a|+\log^{+}|b|, we have log+|E⁡(x)|≤log+|E⁡(x)​|x|ν+12|+log+⁡||x|−ν−12|\log^{+}|E(x)|\leq\log^{+}\big|E(x)|x|^{\nu+\frac{1}{2}}\big|+\log^{+}\big||x|^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\big| and an application of Jensen’s inequality as in (5.3) yields

∫ℝlog+⁡|E⁡(x)|1+x2​d​x<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\log^{+}|E(x)|}{1+x^{2}}\,\text{\rm d}x<\infty.

From Lemma 8 we see that EE has bounded type in ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+} (condition (C1)), and moreover, since H=ℋ⁡(Eν)H=\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) as sets, with the aid of Lemma 9 we conclude that τ⁡(E)=τ⁡(K⁡(0,⋅))≤1\tau(E)=\tau(K(0,\cdot))\leq 1. In fact, we must have τ⁡(E)=1\tau(E)=1, since by Lemma 9 the space H=ℋ⁡(Eν)=ℋ⁡(E)H=\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu})=\mathcal{H}(E) admits only functions FF with τ⁡(F)≤τ⁡(E)\tau(F)\leq\tau(E), and we know from the start that there exist functions in F∈ℋ⁡(Eν)F\in\mathcal{H}(E_{\nu}) with exponential type equal to 11. Finally, condition (C4) follows from Lemma 10 applied to EνE_{\nu} or EE, depending if we start with the left-hand side or the right-hand side of (1.5) being finite, and the fact that HH is isometric to ℋ⁡(E)\mathcal{H}(E).
